beats.intro: Derivatives, module ten. [[sub]]To price an option, we need a model of how the underlying can move. The simplest one has just two outcomes.
beats.tree: [[a]]Forwards can be priced without any view on future prices. Options cannot, because their payoff depends on where the price ends up. The one-period binomial model gives the underlying just two outcomes. [[up]]Today the price is eighty euros. In one year it goes up to a hundred ten, a gross return of one point three seven five. [[down]]Or it goes down to sixty, a gross return of point seven five. The gap between the two outcomes sets the volatility. [[call]]Take a one-year call with an exercise price of a hundred. If the price rises, the call pays ten. If it falls, the call pays nothing. [[q]]We never need to know the probability of an up move. Only the two outcomes matter.
beats.hedge: [[a]]To price the call, build a portfolio that has no risk. Sell the call, and buy h units of the underlying. [[eq]]Choose h so the portfolio is worth the same in both scenarios. The hedge ratio is the difference in option payoffs, divided by the difference in underlying prices. [[calc]]Here that is ten minus zero, over a hundred ten minus sixty: point two. [[up]]If the price rises, the portfolio is point two times a hundred ten, minus the ten owed on the call: twelve euros. [[dn]]If it falls, it is point two times sixty: twelve euros. [[pt]]Twelve euros in every scenario: a risk-free payoff.
beats.price: [[a]]A risk-free portfolio must earn the risk-free rate, otherwise there is an arbitrage. So today's value is the twelve euros, discounted. [[rate]]With a rate of five percent, that is eleven euros forty-three. [[c0]]The portfolio holds point two shares worth sixteen euros, minus the call. So the call is worth sixteen, minus eleven forty-three: four euros fifty-seven. [[chk]]Check: eleven forty-three growing at five percent is twelve euros. The hedged portfolio earns exactly the risk-free rate.
beats.example: [[a]]Hightest Capital sells a call on a fifty-dollar stock, with an exercise price of fifty-five and a rate of five percent. [[s20]]If the stock moves up or down twenty percent, it ends at sixty or forty. The call pays five or nothing. The hedge ratio is point two five, the hedged portfolio is worth ten, and today that is nine fifty-two. The call is worth twelve fifty minus nine fifty-two: two dollars ninety-eight. [[s40]]If the stock moves forty percent, it ends at seventy or thirty. The call pays fifteen or nothing. The hedge ratio is point three seven five, the portfolio is worth eleven twenty-five, and the call is worth eight dollars and four cents. [[vol]]More volatility, a higher call price. [[view]]And if Hightest believes the stock is more likely to rise? The price does not change. The hedge removes any dependence on direction. [[put]]Using put-call parity, the puts are worth five thirty-six, and ten forty-two.
beats.rn: [[a]]There is a shortcut. The call value is the expected payoff, discounted at the risk-free rate, using risk-neutral probabilities. [[pi]]The risk-neutral probability of an up move is one plus the rate, minus the down return, divided by the up return minus the down return. [[ex1]]For the eighty euro stock, that is one point oh five minus point seven five, over one point three seven five minus point seven five: point four eight. The call is point four eight times ten, over one point oh five: four fifty-seven. The same answer. [[ex2]]For Hightest at twenty percent, the probability is point six two five, and the call is three twenty-five, over one point oh five: two ninety-eight. [[pt]]These are not real-world probabilities. Neither the real probabilities, nor the stock's expected return, are needed. Only the up and down returns, and the risk-free rate.
beats.put: [[a]]The same method prices a put. A stock is at twenty pounds, the put has an exercise price of twenty-one, and the stock moves ten percent either way, over six months. [[pay]]At twenty-two, the put pays nothing. At eighteen, it pays three pounds. [[h]]The hedge ratio is negative point seven five: buy the put, and also buy point seven five shares. [[v1]]In both scenarios, the portfolio is worth sixteen pounds fifty. [[v0]]Discounted at four percent for six months, that is sixteen eighteen today. [[res]]Subtract point seven five shares, worth fifteen pounds. The put is worth one pound eighteen.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]An option needs a model for the underlying's price, and the binomial model gives it two outcomes. [[w2]]Selling a call and buying h shares creates a risk-free portfolio, which must earn the risk-free rate. [[w3]]Equivalently, price the option as its discounted expected payoff under risk-neutral probabilities. [[w4]]The real probabilities do not matter. Volatility, through the up and down returns, does.
beats.finish: Module ten complete. The derivatives section is finished. Next: alternative investments.
